title: A first Australian nuclear power reactor could not be generating electricity before 2040
oneLiner: Legislation, licensing, site selection, workforce and construction each take years, and none has started.
body: Starting from no regulator for power reactors, no licensed site and no construction supply chain, the sequence of repeal, regulatory design, licensing, approvals and a first-of-a-kind build is estimated by CSIRO and others at fifteen years or more. On that reckoning a decision taken now delivers first power around 2040 at the earliest.
contextBackground: This is the pivot of the whole nuclear debate: both sides agree the grid needs firm low-emissions capacity, and they divide on whether nuclear could arrive in time to supply it. Most of the arguments about cost and about coal closures draw their force from this one estimate.
contextDisagreement: Supporters of the estimate point to the sequence of steps and to comparable first builds. Critics argue a determined government using a proven reactor design and existing coal sites could compress the timeline, and that estimates for first-of-a-kind builds are inherently pessimistic.

otherClaim.title: Nuclear power cannot help with Australia's electricity prices or reliability in time to matter

claimItself.title: Nuclear power cannot help with Australia's electricity prices or reliability in time to matter
claimItself.oneLiner: The pressure on bills and on the grid is this decade; a first reactor is the decade after next.
claimItself.body: The case for repeal is usually made in terms of today's problems: high bills, coal plants closing, a grid under strain. Each of those plays out in the 2020s and 2030s. Even on generous assumptions nothing nuclear would generate before 2040, by which time the coal fleet has closed and the firming it needed has been built from something else.

otherClaim.title: Australia has no licensing regime, construction supply chain or operating workforce for nuclear power reactors

claimItself.title: Australia has no licensing regime, construction supply chain or operating workforce for nuclear power reactors
claimItself.oneLiner: The national regulator licenses research reactors and medical facilities, not power plants.
claimItself.body: The Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency regulates one research reactor at Lucas Heights and radiation use in medicine and industry. It has no framework for licensing, inspecting or decommissioning a power reactor, and no Australian firm has built one. Each of these would have to be created before construction could begin.

otherClaim.title: The 2020 independent review of the EPBC Act found its approval processes slow, duplicative and unpredictable

claimItself.title: The 2020 independent review of the EPBC Act found its approval processes slow, duplicative and unpredictable
claimItself.oneLiner: The government's own review reached the conclusion industry had been making for years.
claimItself.body: The review, led by Professor Graeme Samuel, found that assessment and approval under the Act duplicated state processes, took far longer than the statutory timeframes suggested, and gave proponents little certainty about what would be required of them.

otherClaim.title: The United Arab Emirates went from deciding to build nuclear power to first grid electricity in about twelve years, with no prior nuclear industry

claimItself.title: The United Arab Emirates went from deciding to build nuclear power to first grid electricity in about twelve years, with no prior nuclear industry
claimItself.oneLiner: The Barakah project is the clearest recent case of a newcomer country building reactors from a standing start.
claimItself.body: The UAE adopted its nuclear policy in 2008, created a regulator and a utility, selected a Korean reactor design, and connected the first of four Barakah units to the grid in 2020. It did so with imported expertise and a vendor delivering a design already operating elsewhere.
